Suppose your computer has IP = 192.168.1.10 and Subnet = 192.168.1.0/24, and Google's IP is something completely different. My network: 192.168.1.10 AND 255.255.255.0 = 192.168.1.0 Google: 142.250.x.x AND 255.255.255.0 = 142.250.x.0 different → remote Your computer determines: Google is outside my subnet → send the packet to the default gateway. So your computer needs the MAC address of the router/default gateway, not Google's MAC address.

Suppose the gateway is 192.168.1.1. Your computer checks its ARP cache. If not present: ARP Request (broadcast to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF): "Who has 192.168.1.1?" ARP Reply (unicast): "192.168.1.1 is at AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF" Now your computer knows the gateway's MAC. Very important interview point You do not ARP for Google's MAC address. You ARP for the default gateway's MAC, because MAC addresses are only relevant to the current local link.

Since HTTPS normally uses TCP for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, TCP connection establishment happens before HTTP data transfer. Client Server SYN ------------------> <---------------- SYN + ACK ACK ------------------> Client: SYN, Seq = 100 Server: SYN + ACK, Seq = 500, Ack = 101 Client: ACK, Ack = 501 → TCP connection established Details and the interactive version: 3-way handshake chapter.

Because the URL is https://, we need TLS. High-level: Client → ClientHello (+ key share, SNI = google.com) Server → ServerHello + Certificate + key-exchange information Client/Server → establish shared session keys The browser verifies the server certificate. The certificate helps establish: "This public key belongs to google.com." Then both sides derive symmetric session keys. Asymmetric cryptography Authentication + key establishment Symmetric cryptography Actual HTTP data. Why? Because it is much faster for bulk data.

Now the browser can send the actual HTTP request. Conceptually: GET / HTTP/2 Host: google.com The HTTP data is encrypted by TLS. So what travels through the network is roughly: encrypted HTTP data → TCP segment → IP packet → Ethernet frame.

This is a very common interview question. At the sender HTTP data TLS encrypted data TCP segment IP packet Ethernet frame Bits At the receiver Bits Ethernet frame IP packet TCP segment TLS HTTP This is encapsulation and decapsulation.

Your computer sends the Ethernet frame to the switch. The frame contains Source MAC = your computer, Destination MAC = router. The switch checks its MAC table and forwards the frame toward the router (on Wi-Fi, the access point plays this role). Remember Switch → MAC address Router → IP address

The router receives the Ethernet frame. It removes the incoming link-layer header/trailer and examines the IP packet. It checks its routing table: Destination IP Longest Prefix Match Next Hop Outgoing Interface Then it creates a new link-layer frame for the next hop. Very important: at every router MAC addresses → change IP source/destination → normally remain the same TTL → decreases (and the header checksum is recomputed) Example: PC → Router A → Router B → Router C → Google. MAC addresses are different on each link. See it field by field in the hop-by-hop diagram. + Added Between your ISP and Google, the path is chosen by BGP (between autonomous systems); inside each network, by an IGP like OSPF.

If you're using a private IP (192.168.1.10), your home router may perform NAT: 192.168.1.10:5000 ↓ NAT Public_IP:30001 The Internet generally sees the public address, not your private address. NAT keeps track of the mapping so replies can return to the correct internal device.

Internet Google network Load balancer / frontend infrastructure Appropriate server The server processes the request. It may need to retrieve data from other internal services/databases, depending on the request. + Added In reality you probably reached a Google edge location close to you (DNS and anycast pick it). The frontend terminates TLS and a reverse proxy / L7 load balancer forwards the request to a backend over Google's private network. See proxies, load balancers and CDNs.

The server sends an HTTP response, for example HTTP/2 200 OK. The response is wrapped the same way: HTTP TLS encryption TCP IP Link-layer frame It travels back through the network (NAT translates the destination back to 192.168.1.10:5000 at your router). TCP provides: ordering acknowledgements retransmission when needed flow control congestion control

Those requests can reuse connections depending on the protocol and browser/server behaviour (keep-alive in HTTP/1.1, multiplexed streams in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3). + Added Rendering pipeline in one line: parse HTML → DOM, parse CSS → CSSOM, combine into the render tree → layout → paint → composite. If the interviewer asks "What happens when you type https://google.com?", a good structured answer: 12-point answer Browser checks caches and performs DNS resolution. DNS gives the server IP address. Client checks whether the destination is local; if remote, it needs the default gateway's MAC using ARP. TCP 3-way handshake establishes the connection. TLS handshake authenticates the server and establishes encryption keys. Browser sends an encrypted HTTP request. Data is encapsulated as TCP segment → IP packet → Ethernet frame. Switches forward using MAC addresses. Routers forward using IP addresses and routing tables. NAT may translate the private source IP to a public IP. Server processes the request and sends the response. TCP delivers it reliably, TLS decrypts it, and the browser renders the response. + Added · HTTP/3 changes the middle With HTTP/3 the browser uses QUIC over UDP (port 443) instead of TCP + TLS. QUIC merges the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into one round trip (0-RTT when resuming), so steps 4 and 5 collapse into one. Browsers learn a site supports HTTP/3 from the Alt-Svc header or a DNS HTTPS record, and fall back to TCP if UDP is blocked.

Q1. Does the client find Google's MAC address? No. It finds the MAC of the next-hop router / default gateway. Q2. Does the MAC address remain the same across the Internet? No. MAC changes at every Layer-2 hop. Q3. Does the IP address change at every router? Normally no. Source/destination IP remain the same end-to-end, except things like NAT can modify them. Q4. Which device uses MAC addresses for forwarding? Switch. Q5. Which device uses IP addresses for routing? Router. Q6. Why TCP before TLS? For the traditional TLS-over-TCP setup used by HTTPS with HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, TCP provides the reliable transport first; TLS needs an ordered, reliable byte stream to run its handshake on. HTTP/3 is different: it uses QUIC over UDP. Q7. Where does DNS fit if the IP is already cached? + Added It is skipped: a browser/OS/resolver cache hit returns the IP immediately, until the record's TTL expires. Q8. What does the server see as the client's IP? + Added Your router's public IP (after NAT), or a carrier-grade NAT address, or the VPN server's IP if you use a VPN. Never 192.168.x.x.

Tap a question to reveal the answer. Say the answer out loud before opening it. Foundations & models What is the difference between the OSI and TCP/IP models? OSI is a 7-layer reference model (Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical). TCP/IP is the 4-layer model the Internet actually uses (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access): it merges the top three OSI layers into Application and the bottom two into Network Access. What is encapsulation? Each layer adds its own header going down: Data → TCP segment → IP packet → Ethernet frame (+FCS) → bits. The receiver strips them going up (decapsulation). Logically each layer talks to its peer layer; physically data goes down, across and up. Which layer does each device work at? Hub and repeater: Layer 1 (bits). Switch and bridge: Layer 2 (MAC). Router: Layer 3 (IP). L4/L7 load balancers and firewalls work higher up. Transmission delay vs propagation delay? Transmission delay = L/R: time to push all bits onto the link; depends on packet size and bandwidth. Propagation delay = d/v: time for a bit to travel the distance; depends on distance and medium, not size. Circuit switching vs packet switching? Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path and fixed bandwidth before sending (old telephone network). Packet switching splits data into packets forwarded independently over shared links (store-and-forward), giving better utilisation but variable delay (the Internet). Data link & medium access How does a switch learn MAC addresses? It learns from the SOURCE MAC of each incoming frame (MAC → arrival port) and forwards based on the DESTINATION MAC. Unknown or broadcast destinations are flooded out every port except the one the frame came in on. Collision domain vs broadcast domain? A collision domain is where frames can collide; a switch gives each port its own. A broadcast domain is everyone who receives a Layer-2 broadcast; only routers (or VLANs) split it. What is a VLAN and why use it? A Virtual LAN splits one physical switch into separate Layer-2 networks (each its own broadcast domain) using 802.1Q tags. Used for isolation (HR vs guests), smaller broadcast domains and flexible grouping; inter-VLAN traffic needs a router or L3 switch. Why is STP needed? Redundant switch links form loops; Ethernet frames have no TTL, so broadcasts circulate forever (broadcast storm). STP elects a root bridge and blocks redundant ports so the active topology is a loop-free tree. Why does Ethernet have a minimum frame size of 64 bytes? So that a sender is still transmitting when news of a collision returns: Tt ≥ 2·Tp. At 10 Mbps with a 51.2 µs slot that is 512 bits = 64 bytes; short payloads are padded. Explain binary exponential backoff. After the n-th collision a station waits K slot times, with K chosen randomly from 0 to 2^min(n,10) − 1. The range doubles each time, which makes repeat collisions less likely. It gives up after 16 attempts. Why does Wi-Fi use CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD? A wireless radio can't detect a collision while transmitting (its own signal drowns everything, and the collision happens at the receiver, which it may not hear). So Wi-Fi avoids collisions with random backoff, uses ACKs to detect failure, and optionally RTS/CTS. What is the hidden terminal problem and how is it solved? A and C can both reach B but can't hear each other, so both sense "free" and collide at B. RTS/CTS fixes it: B's CTS is heard by C, which stays silent for the announced duration. CRC vs checksum vs Hamming code? Checksum: 1's-complement sum, cheap, used by IP/TCP/UDP, detection only. CRC: polynomial XOR division, strong detection including burst errors, used by Ethernet FCS. Hamming: places parity bits at powers of 2 and can correct a single-bit error using the syndrome. Network layer What does ARP do? Is the request broadcast or unicast? ARP maps an IPv4 address to a MAC on the local link. The request ("Who has 192.168.1.20?") is broadcast; the reply is unicast. Results go in the ARP cache. IPv6 uses NDP instead. Your PC sends a packet to a server on another network. Whose MAC does it put in the frame? The default gateway's (router's) MAC, found with ARP. The destination IP is still the server's. Which addresses change as a packet crosses routers? The MAC addresses change at every hop (new frame per link). Source and destination IP stay the same end-to-end, except where NAT rewrites them. TTL decreases by 1 per router. What is NAT and why is it used? Network Address Translation rewrites private source addresses (and ports, in PAT) to a public IP at the router and keeps a translation table so replies come back. It lets many devices share one public IPv4 address, conserving addresses; side-effect: breaks end-to-end connectivity (needs port forwarding). What is longest prefix match? When several routing-table entries match a destination, the router uses the most specific (longest prefix): /24 beats /16 beats /8, and 0.0.0.0/0 (default route) matches only if nothing else does. What is TTL and why does it exist? An 8-bit IP header field decremented by every router; at 0 the packet is dropped and an ICMP Time Exceeded is sent. It stops packets looping forever. (DNS TTL is something else: a cache lifetime in seconds.) How does traceroute work? It sends probes with TTL = 1, 2, 3…; each router where TTL hits 0 replies with ICMP Time Exceeded, revealing itself. The destination finally replies (ICMP echo reply or port unreachable). How many usable hosts in a /26? Which subnet is 192.168.10.77/26 in? 2^6 − 2 = 62 hosts. Block size 64, so 77 is in 192.168.10.64/26: broadcast .127, usable .65–.126. Why was IPv6 introduced and what else changed? IPv4's 32-bit space ran out. IPv6 has 128-bit addresses, a fixed 40-byte header without checksum, no broadcast, no router fragmentation, NDP instead of ARP, SLAAC autoconfiguration, and no need for NAT. How does IP fragmentation work? A router splits a packet larger than the next link's MTU; all fragments share the Identification field, MF = 1 on all but the last, and the offset is in 8-byte units. Only the destination reassembles. If DF is set the router drops it and sends ICMP "fragmentation needed" (Path MTU Discovery). Distance vector vs link state? Why does OSPF converge faster than RIP? DV routers share distance tables with neighbours (Bellman-Ford, RIP); LS routers flood link-state adverts so everyone has the full map and runs Dijkstra (OSPF). OSPF reacts to changes immediately with a full view, while DV spreads information hop by hop on timers and can count to infinity. What is the count-to-infinity problem? In distance vector routing, after a link fails, routers keep believing each other's stale routes and increase the metric step by step (2, 3, 4…) until reaching "infinity" (16 in RIP). Fixes: split horizon, poison reverse, triggered updates, hold-down timers. What is BGP and why is it "policy-based"? BGP is the path-vector protocol that routes between autonomous systems (over TCP 179). Routes are chosen by business policy and attributes (AS_PATH, LOCAL_PREF, MED), not just shortest path; AS_PATH also prevents loops. Transport layer TCP vs UDP: when would you choose UDP? When low latency matters more than perfect delivery or the app handles reliability itself: DNS queries, DHCP, VoIP, video calls, online games, live streaming, and QUIC/HTTP/3. What uniquely identifies a TCP connection? The 4-tuple: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port (plus protocol: 5-tuple). That's how one server port 443 serves thousands of clients. Explain the TCP 3-way handshake. Why not 2-way? SYN (Seq = x) → SYN-ACK (Seq = y, Ack = x+1) → ACK (Ack = y+1). Both sides must exchange and confirm their initial sequence numbers and prove both directions work; with only two messages the server never learns the client received its SYN-ACK, and old duplicate SYNs could open ghost connections. Client sends SYN with Seq = 100. What ACK number does the server send? 101, because the SYN consumes one sequence number (FIN does too). What is a SYN flood and how do SYN cookies help? An attacker sends many SYNs and never completes the handshake, filling the server's half-open connection queue. SYN cookies encode the connection state in the server's ISN, so the server keeps no memory until a valid ACK arrives. Flow control vs congestion control? Flow control protects the receiver using rwnd (advertised by the receiver). Congestion control protects the network using cwnd (computed by the sender). The sender may have min(rwnd, cwnd) bytes in flight. How does TCP detect packet loss? Two ways: a retransmission timeout (RTO expires with no ACK) and three duplicate ACKs (triggers fast retransmit). RTO = EstimatedRTT + 4·DevRTT. Go-Back-N vs Selective Repeat? Which does TCP use? GBN resends the lost packet and everything after it; SR resends only the lost one and buffers out-of-order packets. TCP is a hybrid: cumulative ACKs like GBN, but receivers buffer out-of-order data and SACK lets it resend only the gaps. Explain slow start and congestion avoidance. Slow start doubles cwnd every RTT (exponential) from a small start until it reaches ssthresh; then congestion avoidance adds about 1 MSS per RTT (linear). On loss, ssthresh = cwnd/2. Tahoe vs Reno on 3 duplicate ACKs? Tahoe sets cwnd = 1 MSS and restarts slow start. Reno halves cwnd (cwnd ≈ ssthresh) and enters fast recovery. Both go to cwnd = 1 on a timeout. Why 4-way termination and not 3? TCP is full-duplex; each direction closes independently. The server ACKs the client's FIN immediately but may keep sending data (half-close), and sends its own FIN later. If it has nothing left, the ACK and FIN can be combined. What is TIME_WAIT and why 2MSL? The active closer waits 2 × Maximum Segment Lifetime after its final ACK so that (1) delayed old segments die before the same 4-tuple is reused and (2) it can re-send the final ACK if the peer's FIN is retransmitted. FIN vs RST? FIN is a graceful close after all data is delivered. RST aborts immediately (closed port, error, application abort), discarding buffered data, with no TIME_WAIT. Application layer & security How does DNS resolution work? Browser cache → OS cache → recursive resolver. If the resolver has no cached answer it queries iteratively: root (→ .com TLD server) → TLD (→ authoritative server) → authoritative (→ A record). The resolver caches the answer for its TTL and returns it. Does DNS use TCP or UDP? Both, port 53. UDP for normal queries; TCP for zone transfers and responses too large for UDP. (DoT uses 853, DoH uses 443.) Explain DHCP DORA. Why is Discover a broadcast? Discover (broadcast) → Offer → Request (broadcast) → ACK, over UDP 67/68. The client has no IP and doesn't know the server, so it must broadcast; the Request is broadcast so other offering servers know they weren't chosen. What does "HTTP is stateless" mean, and how do sites keep you logged in? Each request is independent; the server keeps no memory of earlier ones. State is added with cookies (a session ID pointing to server-side session data) or tokens like JWT sent in each request. Which HTTP methods are idempotent? GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS (GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are also safe). POST is neither safe nor idempotent; PATCH isn't guaranteed to be idempotent. 502 vs 503 vs 504? 502 Bad Gateway: the proxy got an invalid response from the upstream server. 503 Service Unavailable: the server is overloaded or down for maintenance. 504 Gateway Timeout: the proxy didn't get a response from upstream in time. What changed in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3? HTTP/2: binary framing, many streams multiplexed over one TCP connection, HPACK header compression. HTTP/3: runs on QUIC over UDP, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream (no TCP head-of-line blocking), with TLS 1.3 built in and faster setup. Does HTTPS encrypt data with the server's public key? No, not the bulk data. Public-key crypto authenticates the server (certificate) and establishes keys (ECDHE); the actual HTTP data is encrypted with fast symmetric session keys (AES-GCM, ChaCha20). How does the browser know the certificate is genuine? It checks the chain server cert → intermediate CA → a root CA in its trust store, verifying each signature, the validity dates, that the domain matches (SAN), and revocation status. What is forward secrecy? Using ephemeral (EC)DHE keys per session, so stealing the server's long-term private key later doesn't let an attacker decrypt previously recorded sessions. TLS 1.3 always provides it. What is a man-in-the-middle attack and how does TLS prevent it? An attacker sits between client and server and impersonates each. TLS prevents it because the attacker can't present a valid, CA-signed certificate for the real domain, so certificate validation fails (HSTS stops downgrade to HTTP). Forward proxy vs reverse proxy vs load balancer vs CDN? A forward proxy acts for clients (the server sees the proxy). A reverse proxy acts for servers (clients see one endpoint) and can load balance, terminate TLS and cache. A load balancer spreads requests across servers (L4 or L7). A CDN caches content at edge servers near users. Stateless vs stateful firewall? A stateless packet filter judges each packet alone by IP/port/protocol rules. A stateful firewall tracks connections and automatically allows the replies to traffic that was allowed out. DoS vs DDoS, and how do you defend? DoS floods a target from one source; DDoS uses many (a botnet), so blocking one IP doesn't help. Defences: rate limiting, SYN cookies, CDN/anycast absorption, scrubbing services, autoscaling. Wireless, VPN, big picture What is the difference between tunneling and a VPN? Tunneling is the technique of putting a packet inside another packet (GRE, 6in4), with no encryption by itself. A VPN is a service built on tunneling plus authentication and encryption/integrity (IPsec, OpenVPN, WireGuard). IPsec transport mode vs tunnel mode? Transport mode protects only the payload and keeps the original IP header (host-to-host). Tunnel mode encrypts the entire original packet and adds a new outer IP header (gateway-to-gateway, site-to-site VPNs). 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz Wi-Fi? 2.4 GHz: longer range and better wall penetration, but slower and crowded (only 3 non-overlapping channels: 1, 6, 11). 5 GHz (and 6 GHz): faster, many more channels, shorter range. WEP vs WPA2 vs WPA3? WEP (RC4) is broken. WPA2 uses AES-CCMP and is still common. WPA3 replaces the pre-shared-key handshake with SAE, which resists offline password guessing and gives forward secrecy. What happens when you type https://google.com? (short version) DNS lookup → check if remote → ARP for the gateway MAC → TCP handshake → TLS handshake (certificate check, session keys) → encrypted HTTP GET → encapsulated into segment/packet/frame → switch (MAC) → routers (IP, MAC rewritten, TTL−1) with NAT at home → Google load balancer → server → response back → browser decrypts and renders. Go up the layers: link up and valid IP (ipconfig) → ping gateway → ping 8.8.8.8 → DNS (nslookup) → port reachable (curl / nc) → TLS and HTTP status (curl -v). The first failing layer is your problem.
